WY-2026-HB10.s: The bill would set rules for county libraries and school libraries on minors' access to sexually explicit materials. It would also define key terms, create a way to sue over violations, and set penalties. The changes would affect libraries and schools in Wyoming.

WY-2026-HB102.s: Wyoming passed a law that creates crimes tied to AI-made sexual images, child sexual images, and AI tools meant to promote self-harm. It also says a person cannot avoid criminal charges by saying an AI tool was used, and it limits when an AI developer can be held liable for harm caused by someone else using the system. The law also updates the child sexual exploitation law to cover child sexual images made with AI.

WY-2026-HB103.s: The bill would create a state law that gives immunity from some lawsuits tied to free speech, free assembly, religious freedom, and petition rights. It would also set rules and limits for lawsuits based on public participation, which means taking part in public issues or speaking out on them. The law would apply in civil cases, which are non-criminal lawsuits, and would take effect on the date set in the bill.

WY-2026-HB105.s: Becomes law and funds K-12 school buildings and other school facility projects in Wyoming for the rest of fiscal year 2025-2026 and for 2027-2028. It sets aside money for school repairs, design, construction, demolition, charter school leases, and school safety and security projects, and it also adds money for major maintenance payments. It also requires the School Facilities Commission to make a priority list for safety and security fixes and report on spending and project progress to state leaders and the governor.

WY-2026-HB106.s: The law adds two full-time jobs in the State Forestry Division, with one starting April 1, 2026 and the other on April 1, 2027. It also sets aside $499,709 from the state general fund for these positions, equipment, and related costs for the State Forestry Conservation Inmate Crew Program.

WY-2026-HB107.s: This act requires an annual transfer of 8% of certain state sales and use tax collections from the General Fund to the Office of State Lands and Investments for cities, towns, and counties. It sets a formula for how the money is divided and requires payments on October 15 and March 15 each year. It also states that the funds should not be used for salary adjustments, more personnel, higher personnel benefits, or some board compensation.

WY-2026-HB111.s: The act became law and sets aside money for state building projects run by the State Construction Department, including some community college, military, agriculture, and health projects. It also funds planning studies, major repairs to state buildings, and work on veteran home facilities, with amounts listed in general, federal, and other funds. It also allows land buying for a future state prison and spending for the Wyoming State Shooting Complex.

WY-2026-HB112.s: This bill would end the Riverton State Office Task Force on April 1, 2026, instead of June 30, 2028. It would also move any unspent money from the $50,000 task force fund back to the Legislative Stabilization Reserve Account on June 30, 2026. The bill became law.

WY-2026-HB116.s: The bill would say that destroying water is not a beneficial use. It would let officials reject some water-use applications, with one exception. The measure also sets when it would apply.

WY-2026-HB120.s: The bill became law and sets up industrial zones to support making value-added products from natural gas. It gives the Wyoming Energy Authority a role in approving these zones, helping with faster permits, and certifying products that meet methane intensity standards. It also gives tax breaks for machinery used in these zones and provides money for the authority to carry out the law.

WY-2026-HB122.s: The act creates Wyoming’s rural health transformation program and sets up an advisory committee to help run it. It creates funds for hospital aid, EMS, workforce training, and other health projects, and it would use federal money for those efforts. It also sets reporting rules, an online reporting portal, and directs state agencies and lawmakers to study related health topics.

WY-2026-HB126.s: This law limits abortions in Wyoming by requiring a check for a detectable fetal heartbeat before an abortion, except in a medical emergency. It also sets other abortion rules, including limits after viability, steps for care of a baby born alive after an abortion attempt, and notice rules for minors and before the procedure. Breaking these rules can be a felony and can also lead to medical license discipline.

WY-2026-HB128.s: Wyoming would exempt certain oil from the 2% severance tax when it comes from certified enhanced oil recovery projects. The exemption would apply to projects certified from July 1, 2026 through July 1, 2031, and it would last five years from the first tertiary production from the project. The Department of Revenue and the Oil and Gas Conservation Commission would have to report each year on the oil that qualifies for the tax break until November 1, 2036.

WY-2026-HB130.s: The bill would change Wyoming’s Second Amendment Protection Act, which is the state law tied to gun rights. It would add some exceptions, set civil and criminal penalties, and create an exception to the Wyoming Governmental Claims Act, which covers claims against the state. It would also add definitions and make related wording changes in other laws.

WY-2026-HB141.s: Would bar cities, towns, and counties from charging fees or adding housing-related conditions to some residential or commercial building projects. It would apply to local governments and to development projects covered by the bill.

WY-2026-HB145.s: This act changes how Wyoming collects taxes and reports for alternative fuels, including electricity used at DC fast charging stations. It adds a license tax on electricity sold for charging plug-in hybrid and all-electric vehicles at those stations, and it requires the price per kilowatt hour to be clearly displayed with taxes included. It also exempts sales of alternative fuels from sales tax. The act lowers the annual decal fee for all-electric vehicles and creates a new annual decal fee for plug-in hybrid vehicles.

WY-2026-HB157.s: The bill would create a way for people to sue if their parental rights are infringed. It would also make an exception to government immunity and remove some government notice rules for those claims. It would affect parents and government bodies.

WY-2026-HB16.s: Wyoming lets the Secretary of State charge a fee of up to $5,000 to speed up filings for business records, property, trademarks, service marks, and trade names. The office must set the fee and the process by rule. Faster filing does not change who has rights based on filing order.

WY-2026-HB178.s: It would bar public employers and certain groups from automatically taking union dues and similar fees from paychecks in the ways named in the bill. It also sets penalties and changes some word meanings in the law. The measure passed the legislature but was vetoed by the governor.

WY-2026-HB2.s: Wyoming lawmakers passed this measure, and it became law. It sets deadlines and steps that local governments must follow when they review some home building permit requests, including telling people if an application is complete and giving written reasons if it is denied. It also allows a review pause when more state or federal approval is needed, cuts the fee by 10% if new requirements are added later in some cases, and says a permit is approved if the deadline is missed. Homes approved this way still must pass safety and code checks before someone can get a certificate to live in them.

WY-2026-HB23.s: The law requires school districts to let children who are not enrolled in the district take part in school club and team activities. It applies to public school cocurricular and extracurricular activities, which are activities tied to school or outside the regular class day. The bill was signed into law.

WY-2026-HB24.s: The law gives charter school reviewers up to 120 days to hold public hearings and decide on new applications. It applies to new charter school applications filed on or after the law’s effective date.

WY-2026-HB25.s: Wyoming made changes to the Wyoming's Tomorrow scholarship program. It removes the rule that students must stay enrolled without a break to keep the scholarship, and it repeals one part of state law. The bill became law.

WY-2026-HB26.s: This act became law and exempts motor vehicles owned by the tribal governments of the Eastern Shoshone and Northern Arapaho tribes on the Wind River Indian Reservation from county and state vehicle registration fees. It also requires the Wyoming Department of Transportation to issue special license plates showing that the vehicles are publicly owned.

WY-2026-HB28.s: This law changes the definition of “explicit sexual conduct” in Wyoming’s child sexual exploitation law. It affects cases involving the sexual exploitation of children. It also includes an effective date.

WY-2026-HB3.s: Wyoming law now says the state and some local governments cannot make rules that single out pregnancy centers for oversight or regulation because they oppose abortion. It also sets out definitions, penalties, and related changes to other laws. The bill became law on March 6, 2026.

WY-2026-HB32.s: The law says commercial motor vehicle drivers in Wyoming must be able to show they can speak English well enough to operate the vehicle. Drivers who do not meet that rule can be fined $1,000 and barred from driving a commercial motor vehicle until they can show English proficiency. If a driver keeps driving after being barred, the driver can be charged with a misdemeanor and fined $1,000 again. The Wyoming Highway Patrol, other state transportation officers, and local peace officers can enforce the law and give citations.

WY-2026-HB36.s: The law creates 24 employee positions in the State Forestry Division for wildland fire suppression, including full-time and temporary full-time jobs. It also sets aside $5,144,000 from the state’s general fund to set up two fire suppression teams and pay for staff, equipment, training, and related costs. It affects the State Forestry Division and its wildland fire work.

WY-2026-HB39.s: The law changes how Wyoming treats gun rights restored in another state after a felony conviction. If a person’s firearm rights are restored under the laws of the state where the conviction happened, Wyoming will recognize that for gun rights. It also says that voting, jury service, and holding office are restored only if that other state’s law also restores those rights.

WY-2026-HB41.s: The bill would give a death benefit to the surviving spouses of certain Wyoming law officers killed in the line of duty, including Highway Patrol, Game and Fish, capitol police, and certain Division of Criminal Investigation agents. The payment would be 90% of the officer’s salary, plus 6% more for each child under 18. It has been signed into law.

WY-2026-HB43.s: The law creates crimes for money laundering and illegal investment. It covers handling money or property tied to crime, or arranging transactions to hide where criminal money came from or to avoid required reports. It sets felony penalties of up to 10 years in prison, a fine of up to $10,000, or both, and gives a limited exception for some federally insured financial institutions and their workers.

WY-2026-HB44.s: The bill became law and takes effect on the date set in the act. It updates Wyoming statutes to fix mistaken cross-references, clean up language from earlier laws, and replace old references. It also makes other small revision changes to existing laws.

WY-2026-HB45.s: Wyoming enacted a change to the long-term homeowner property tax exemption. It moves the filing deadline to March 1 each year, limits the exemption to the first $3 million of a home’s fair market value, and lets people keep it by confirming with the assessor’s office each year. It also allows the exemption when a homeowner moves to another home in the state and removes the sunset date for the program.

WY-2026-HB56.s: The bill would repeal low-carbon energy standard rules for public utilities and remove conflicting laws tied to them. It would also make related changes, require new rulemaking, and set an effective date.

WY-2026-HB69.s: The law requires the Department of Health to transfer one state land parcel in Fremont County to the Wyoming Department of Transportation, with the transportation department paying closing and title insurance costs. It also requires the department to transfer another state land parcel, and that land must be used only for homes. The department must work with the city of Lander, the Board of Land Commissioners, and the Office of State Lands and Investments, and the transportation department must report back after the transfers are finished.

WY-2026-HB75.s: Wyoming enacted a law that limits who can own, run, or manage a virtual currency kiosk. Only a licensed money transmitter or a financial institution with a state charter may do so. Running one without approval is a felony with at least 3 years in prison, a fine of at least $10,000, or both, and the state banking commissioner must make rules for approved operators.

WY-2026-HB76.s: This bill would repeal a rule that blocks landowners from objecting to a proposed annexation in some cases, when part of the annexed area borders a city or town. It would apply to annexation cases and includes an effective date.

WY-2026-HB78.s: The bill would create a Forest Health Grant Program run by the State Forester to help pay for projects that improve forest health, water quality, wildfire risk reduction, forest product output, and wildlife habitat. Grants could cover up to 75% of project costs on state, local, or private land, and up to 50% on federal land, with matching funds required. It would also create a fund for the program, require review by the Attorney General, and require yearly reporting on grants awarded. It was signed into law.

WY-2026-HB8.s: Wyoming made stalking a minor a felony when the person doing it is at least 18 years old. That offense can bring up to 10 years in prison. The bill was signed into law.

WY-2026-HB80.s: Wyoming law now lets people who live full time in nursing care or assisted living facilities renew an ID card by mail. They must send an application, pay the fee, and include a notarized statement and other papers that show their information is correct. The new mail-in rule for residents starts July 1, 2026, and the transportation department must make rules to carry it out right away.

WY-2026-HB83.s: The bill would change the penalty for not following a legislative subpoena, which is an order to appear or give information from lawmakers. It affects people who are told to comply with such a subpoena. It also includes an effective date.

WY-2026-HB86.s: The bill would let the secretary of state file a complaint with the governor against a county clerk for breaking election code rules. It affects county clerks and state election officials. It would also set an effective date.

WY-2026-HB87.s: Wyoming would fund and approve several water planning studies, including early review studies and deeper feasibility studies. It also changes an earlier study for the Nowood River Storage–Alkali Creek project. The Water Development Commission must report back to lawmakers on each study before the 2028 session.

WY-2026-HB9.s: Wyoming’s law creates a new crime for grooming a minor for a sex offense. It applies to adults who are at least 4 years older than the minor and who try to push, lure, or trick the minor into sexual conduct, sexual meetings, or explicit material, or who use a position of authority for that purpose. Penalties can include felony prison time, up to 10 years of probation, sex offender treatment, and sex offender registration. The bill was signed into law.

WY-2026-HB92.s: This law bars people who are listed on Wyoming’s sex offender registry from holding certain public offices. Election officials must refuse to certify ineligible candidates, and any office held by a disqualified person is treated as vacant. It applies to people elected or appointed on or after July 1, 2026.

WY-2026-HB96.s: The measure lowers the minimum age for a concealed-carry permit from 21 to 18 in Wyoming. It also removes old rules tied to permits for people ages 18 to 21.

WY-2026-HB98.s: This law makes it a misdemeanor to violate the Prohibit Red Flag Gun Seizure Act. A person who breaks it can face up to one year in jail, a fine of up to $2,000, or both.

WY-2026-SF1.s: The act sets the state budget for Wyoming for the 2026-2028 two-year period. It gives money to state agencies and programs, including health care, K-12 schools, higher education, prisons, and family services, and it also allows some fund transfers and carryover of money. The governor signed it and vetoed some parts, and it became Chapter 44.

WY-2026-SF10.s: Now law, it lets the Department of Health make contracts with counties to pay county jails back for security, exams, or treatment given to an accused person while they wait for evaluation at the state hospital. It also requires the department to report to a legislative committee by October 1, 2027 on which county detention facilities are used and how the contracts are being put into place.

WY-2026-SF100.s: The bill would create a task force to review the Wyoming Business Council and set what it must look at. It would also add certain ex officio members to the council board, spell out more council duties, and require reports. It would include money for the work and set an effective date.

WY-2026-SF101.s: This bill would change Wyoming's Second Amendment Protection Act and add some new exceptions to it. It would also create civil and criminal penalties, define some terms, and make related changes to state law. It would also add an exception to the Wyoming Governmental Claims Act, which is the law about when people can sue the state.

WY-2026-SF102.s: The law requires the Wyoming Energy Authority to study the state’s power lines and future growth in two parts. It would look at three possible growth paths, plan for future transmission needs, and consider new line and power storage technology, then make a short report on public utilities’ role in regional power groups. The first report is due by November 1, 2027, and the second by September 1, 2028; it takes effect right away.

WY-2026-SF105.s: Wyoming changed its real estate rules for brokers and other licensees. It expands who counts as a customer and requires a clear notice that a customer does not have to sign a legal agency agreement just to view or tour property. After a buyer or seller refuses to sign that notice, the licensee may still keep helping the customer. The law takes effect July 1, 2026.

WY-2026-SF106.s: Wyoming enacted changes to how people are checked for SNAP and Medicaid eligibility, including shorter recertification times and more frequent checks of residency, other-state enrollment, and death records. It also limits some Medicaid back pay, restricts waivers of SNAP work rules without legislative approval, and sets citizenship and qualified-alien rules for certain public aid programs. Hospitals and state agencies must report citizenship status, Medicaid eligibility data, fraud cases, and related costs.

WY-2026-SF107.s: Wyoming has enacted a statewide system for motor vehicle registration and license plate issuance. The Wyoming Department of Transportation would run the system, may hire vendors to help, and all county treasurers would have to use it. The department may charge up to $5 per transaction to cover its costs, and the law takes effect July 1, 2028.

WY-2026-SF110.s: The bill would change how residential property tax is handled in Wyoming, including the tax rates for homes. It would also limit some local property tax charges, called mills, to owner-occupied primary homes and repeal one related tax break. The bill would make other related changes and include an appropriation, which is state funding.

WY-2026-SF112.s: The bill would end the rule that license plates must be replaced on a set cycle. It would instead require replacement only in the cases spelled out in the bill, and it would add a fee for replacement plates. It also would define key terms and make related changes to other motor vehicle laws.

WY-2026-SF113.s: The law requires counties to do hand-count checks in the 2026 primary and general elections. Each county must compare those hand counts with machine counts for one federal race, one statewide race, and all legislative races in the county, and may check more races too. It also sets a check of about 5% of ballots cast on election day and about 5% of voting machines, and counties must report any mismatches to state officials.

WY-2026-SF119.s: This bill would repeal the strategic investments and projects account and move any money in it to other state funds. It would also change how much the governor can include in budget recommendations and update where some investment earnings and deposits go. The bill also would remove outdated language and make related changes to other laws.

WY-2026-SF121.s: Wyoming changed its pharmacy law to define what pharmacists do, including reading and checking prescriptions, making and giving out medicine, counseling patients, and working to improve patient safety. It also says pharmacists do not have to take part in collaborative care, and that part will be run by Pharmacy Board rules. The Board of Pharmacy must write any rules needed to carry out the law, which was signed by the governor.

WY-2026-SF123.s: Creates the Wyoming Energy Dominance Fund to give grants and loans for energy research, test projects, pilot projects, and commercial development. The Wyoming Energy Authority would run the fund, use an application process, and tell lawmakers about planned spending. It also lets money be moved into the fund and sets a sunset date of December 31, 2028.

WY-2026-SF14.s: The bill became law and sets aside $240,000 for the state Department of Education. The money would pay for one full-time literacy staff member to help school districts use reading tests, reading help plans, and language and literacy programs for K-3 students.

WY-2026-SF20.s: The act sets rules for how Wyoming government offices handle personal data. It bars them from buying, selling, trading, or passing along personal data except in certain cases, and it lets people ask for copies and challenge errors in data held by state offices. Government entities must also make data policies and explain why they keep personal data for more than three years; the policy requirement starts July 1, 2027.

WY-2026-SF21.s: Wyoming law now creates a reserve account for Wyoming Stable Tokens equal to 2% of the value of all tokens in circulation. It lets the state token commission take in grants and other money, invest some trust funds in money market funds, and use some account money for operating costs under set rules. After those costs, money is moved to the reserve account, saved as allowed by the commission, and the rest goes to the Public School Foundation Program Account each quarter. It also lets the commission make agreements with other states.

WY-2026-SF23.s: The law expands who can do outpatient mental health exams for people being held for involuntary psychiatric care. It adds licensed advanced practice registered nurses, licensed physician assistants, licensed psychiatric-mental health nurse practitioners, and physician assistants with the right education, training, and experience. It was signed by the governor.

WY-2026-SF26.s: The law changes how some Wyoming Game and Fish Commission land is taxed. Starting January 1, 2027, most real property the commission owns would be free from property tax, but land used for wildlife work or employee housing would still be taxed under a special rate. The measure became law.

WY-2026-SF27.s: The bill became law and lets a person use a leashed blood-trailing dog to track and recover a black bear that has been killed or wounded. It affects people who hunt or recover black bears in Wyoming.

WY-2026-SF28.s: The law changes how voting machines and electronic voting systems are tested before elections. It sets rules for public notice, lets representatives and the public be present, and says each machine must be tested and prepared on its own. It also requires test results to be posted and test materials and ballots to be kept, and it lets people challenge machine prep within five days after sealing.

WY-2026-SF35.s: In Wyoming, school district boards would have to set rules for students’ cell phones and smart devices at school. Districts would also have to send in a copy of their policy after it is first adopted and after any big change. The law says a “smart device” does not include a wearable that only tells time, tracks health info, or tracks location.

WY-2026-SF37.s: The bill would raise the school building square footage used to figure routine and major maintenance funding for school districts. It would also provide money for K-12 public school finance. It affects Wyoming school districts and K-12 public schools.

WY-2026-SF39.s: The bill would change the property tax break for long-term homeowners. It would remove the end date for the break, change when people must apply, let them claim it again in later years, and change the amount of the break. It would also set an effective date.

WY-2026-SF4.s: The law raises Medicaid pay for ground ambulance services to 100% of the current Medicare rate. The state health department must also set special Medicaid fee schedules for rural and super-rural ambulance services and report the added costs to two legislative committees. It includes money to help cover the higher payments.

WY-2026-SF41.s: The act lets independent contractors use portable benefit accounts to set aside money for insurance and retirement savings. It allows voluntary deposits from a hiring party or other person, and says those deposits do not decide whether someone is an employee or an independent contractor. The Department of Workforce Services must make rules to carry out the law. Some rulemaking parts took effect right away, and the rest takes effect July 1, 2026.

WY-2026-SF44.s: The act changes Wyoming’s gambling rules. It narrows the social gambling exception to private, non-advertised games tied to a real social relationship, and no one may be paid for helping except by winning. It also says charitable raffles or drawings count only if all net proceeds go to charity, and it defines profit as any financial gain.

WY-2026-SF45.s: This act changes the rules for simulcasting permits in Wyoming. A city, town, or county must approve a simulcasting facility before the commission can issue or renew a permit, and the local authority must give public notice and hold a hearing on the application. The local authority may set reasonable conditions, deny or revoke approval only for good cause, and some decisions can be appealed to district court. People who already hold a simulcasting permit may keep operating through December 31, 2027, before the new requirements apply.

WY-2026-SF46.s: The law limits skill-based amusement games in liquor places to businesses that are licensed to sell alcohol for drinking on the premises. It also requires those games to be kept in the part of the business where alcohol is sold. Existing games in places that do not fit the new rule may keep running under set conditions until the current permit ends.

WY-2026-SF48.s: Wyoming's Stem Cell Freedom Act would let doctors recommend and perform stem cell therapy in certain cases and would allow health insurers, but not require them, to cover it. It would bar the state medical board from disciplining doctors for using or promoting this therapy, block the state from denying patients access to it, and limit lawsuits against people who properly perform it. The law also requires the board to keep a public list of doctors registered to do this therapy.

WY-2026-SF50.s: The law requires the State Engineer to do a groundwater study at least once every 10 years in certain counties with groundwater control areas or corrective controls. The study must look at how those controls work, how much water is recharging the aquifer compared with how much is being used, and how future growth could affect it. Results must be made public, and a report must be sent to a legislative committee within 60 days after the study is done. The first study must be finished by June 30, 2030, and the bill sets aside money for it.

WY-2026-SF54.s: This act creates a way for a special purpose depository institution, a bank with a limited set of powers, to change its charter into a state bank. It also creates a way for a state bank to change its charter into a special purpose depository institution.

WY-2026-SF55.s: Wyoming changed rules for special purpose depository institutions, a kind of bank. It raised the money and plan details needed before one can start business, cut the operating expense estimate from three years to one year, and removed the need for a contingency account. It also set up a fund for possible shutdown costs and lets some state banking decisions be appealed to court.

WY-2026-SF56.s: Kratom products would be regulated in how they are made, sold, advertised, displayed, packed, and delivered. The state health and agriculture departments would get money to carry out the law, and the state chemist could test products to check if they follow the rules. People or stores that break the law could face criminal penalties, and stores could also face court orders if they keep breaking it. A store would not get a criminal fine for a first offense if it has a written rule against selling kratom to people under 21 and makes workers follow it.

WY-2026-SF57.s: Hospitals in Wyoming would have to post prices for medical items and services on their websites. The state Department of Health would watch for compliance and could require a correction plan, fine hospitals, or affect a hospital's license if it does not follow the rules. The law would sunset on July 1, 2029.

WY-2026-SF58.s: This law removes the July 1, 2026 sunset date from the Wyoming Indian Child Welfare Act, so the act will not automatically end on that date. It affects people and agencies involved in child welfare cases for American Indian children in Wyoming.

WY-2026-SF59.s: Creates a Wyoming program for language and reading instruction for students in kindergarten through grade 12. School districts would have to make and follow language and literacy plans, create reading plans for students with reading trouble, and provide staff training. Districts would also report each year on student reading levels and teaching practices, and the state education agency could set up a literacy division to help run the program. It was signed into law as SEA No. 0043.

WY-2026-SF60.s: Would set money for K-12 school building and facility projects for the state budget periods from July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2028, and for the rest of the current budget period ending June 30, 2026. It would also create a grant program for school safety and security projects and set rules school districts would have to meet to get those funds. The bill would require reports and set conditions for how the money could be spent.

WY-2026-SF61.s: The law exempts some motor vehicle sales from excise tax when one immediate family member sells or gives a vehicle to another. It applies to parents, children, spouses, siblings, stepparents, stepchildren, stepsiblings, grandparents, and grandchildren, if the seller already paid the tax when they got the vehicle. The bill was signed into law.

WY-2026-SF66.s: This act lets people with life-threatening illnesses and people who are vision-impaired receive donated hunting licenses, as specified in state rules. It also requires the agency to make rules for how this works. The bill has become law.

WY-2026-SF67.s: The law lets the governor organize and keep a Wyoming State Guard without first activating the Wyoming National Guard for federal service. It gives the governor control over the Guard’s setup, size, training, and gear, and lets it be used for public safety, emergencies, wildland fire response, and other duties the governor assigns. It also sets aside $25,000 from the state’s general fund for a state defense council and for setting up and equipping the Guard.

WY-2026-SF69.s: This law orders a study of public wastewater and stormwater systems in Wyoming. The Department of Environmental Quality will do the study with two other state offices, and cities, towns, special districts, and counties must share data for it. It also sets rules for how the data is kept and who can see it, gives money for the work, and says the department must give yearly progress reports from 2026 to 2030.

WY-2026-SF70.s: Becomes law and updates Wyoming water projects and funding. It sets lists of construction, repair, and water development projects for 2026 and 2027, including pipelines, wells, tanks, and canal work, and it changes several earlier projects. It also allows money to move between two water development accounts, transfers the Sheep Mountain No. 2 test well to the city of Douglas, and orders two studies with reports due to the Select Water Committee in 2026 and 2030.

WY-2026-SF81.s: This law changes how Wyoming funds K-12 public schools and sets rules for how some school money can be used. It gives districts new steps for teacher pay, special education, transportation, retirement, and dual enrollment grants for students taking college courses through a school agreement. It also extends the school finance study committee and adds reporting rules for schools and the state education department.

WY-2026-SF84.s: Creates a voluntary water conservation program for Wyoming’s part of the Colorado River basin, run by the State Engineer. It sets rules for applying for conservation projects, public notice and comments, and approval standards tied to lower water use and Wyoming’s water agreement duties. The law also allows stored conserved water in certain reservoirs, gives funding for the program, and says no water rights are lost by joining it.

WY-2026-SF85.s: This act creates an account to provide a stable funding source for the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force in Wyoming. It appropriates $1,600,000 to the account and says the money is to support the Division of Criminal Investigation’s work against internet crimes against children. The Attorney General must write the rules needed to carry it out.

WY-2026-SF88.s: The act limits where sex offenders can live near child care centers. It bars them from living within 1,000 feet of a child care center, with some older homes and centers covered by an exception. Law enforcement must check sex offender addresses and notify child care centers that are within 1,000 feet of a sex offender's home.

WY-2026-SF90.s: Wyoming law now limits the rent a school district can charge for using district property to the hourly cost of staff, equipment, utilities, and supplies the district actually uses. Schools must give an itemized cost list within 15 days if asked, and they cannot require the renter to be a nonprofit or any other specific type of group. The law does not change contracts or agreements made before July 1, 2026.

WY-2026-SF95.s: Creates a program that lets the Transportation Department use approved third-party providers to handle some driver license and motor vehicle services. It also requires the department to write rules for how the program works. The measure became law in Wyoming.

WY-2026-SF98.s: The bill would have changed Wyoming property tax rules to give an exemption to some state residents who are honorably discharged veterans, current or reserve members of the Wyoming National Guard or U.S. armed forces, and certain surviving spouses or parents. It would also have changed the residency rule and set out definitions and when the change would apply. The bill died in committee before becoming law.

WY-2026-SF99.s: Wyoming passed a law that gives electric utilities a nonexclusive easement, or limited right to use land, for existing power lines and other delivery equipment if certain notice and use rules are met. It applies to systems installed on or before January 1, 2026, that are visible and have been used without a break of more than one year. The utility may maintain, repair, rebuild, and clear hazardous trees or plants, with access limited to what is needed, and the easement cannot extend more than 30 feet from the equipment.

WY-2026-SJ6.s: The resolution would set April 26 each year as Shared Parenting Day in Wyoming. It says shared parenting matters and that children should have good relationships with both parents when both are fit caregivers.

WY-2026-SJ9.s: This resolution asks Congress and federal agencies to respect Wyoming's role in decisions about land in the state, including public lands held by the federal government. It also asks them to respect current land rules and local communities' views on how land use affects them. The measure has passed and was signed into law.
